title: Coil-built sculptural abstract vase
subtitle: An asymmetric hand-built form that explores the coils as a surface feature
excerpt: Most coil pots smooth the coils into the wall to hide the method of construction. This vase keeps the coil ridges visible on the exterior as part of the design. The form is asymmetric by intent: the neck can be pinched narrower on one side, the body leaned slightly to the left or right. Air-dry clay, no kiln required.
sourceNotes: Coil-building technique derived from first principles. Exposed-coil decorative aesthetic documented in mid-twentieth-century studio pottery practice; technique references derived from traditional hand-building methodology.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rope of clay rolled to even diameter, used as the building unit in coil construction.
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to join and trim.
Clay dissolved in water to a thick paste, used as adhesive when joining clay pieces.
Air-dried but unfired clay. Fragile; the final stage before sealing an air-dry piece.

content.text: Coil building is the method by which the oldest large ceramic vessels were made: stacked rings of clay, each ring joined to the one below. Standard instruction tells you to smooth the exterior so the
coil

joins disappear. This tutorial does the opposite: the coils stay visible on the exterior as a spiral ridge, and the only smoothing happens on the interior wall so the form is strong but shows its construction. The result looks deliberately made rather than factory-produced, which is the point.

The form is asymmetric. A tilted neck or an off-centre rim is not a fault in this design: build the tilt in deliberately by pinching one side of the neck narrower before the clay stiffens. The asymmetry is the character of the piece.
What you'll need

Around 600 g of air-dry clay for a vase roughly 18 cm tall with a 10 cm body diameter. Mix a small cup of slurry: a tablespoon of clay dissolved in warm water to the consistency of thin cream. Keep the slurry covered between uses so it does not skin over.
Building the base
Pinch a flat base disc, 8 cm across and 8 mm thick. Pat the edges level with the wooden rib. Score the top surface all over with the needle tool.
Roll a
coil

to 10 mm diameter and 28 cm long between the palms and the work surface. Keep the pressure even so the diameter is consistent along the length. Score both the top of the base and the underside of the coil. Apply
slurry
to both surfaces and press the coil around the rim of the base disc, overlapping the start and end by 2 cm. Blend the overlap with a fingertip.

Blend the interior of the coil-to-base join by pressing with a wooden rib in short downward strokes, pulling the coil clay into the base. The exterior of this first coil can be blended too: the base ring looks better smooth.
Building the body

Roll the next coil: same diameter, long enough to circle the form. Score the top of the previous coil, apply slurry, and press the new coil on top. Blend the interior join only. Leave the exterior coil ridge visible.
Build up five to seven coils this way. As you add each one, curve the form outward slightly by placing each coil fractionally further out than the one below: the body of the vase widens as you build.
Allow the lower half to stiffen to
leather-hard
before continuing: loose coils stack into a wobbly form. Cover the top edge with a damp cloth and leave for 30 minutes while the lower section firms up.

For the neck, place each coil fractionally inward to narrow the form. For the deliberate asymmetry, pinch one side of the neck slightly tighter than the other, or lean the top two coils 5 degrees to one side while the clay is still soft enough to move.
Finish with a final coil at the rim. Smooth the rim flat with a dampened fingertip.
Drying

Coil-built forms dry unevenly. The exposed ridges on the exterior dry faster than the blended interior. Cover the whole piece loosely with a plastic bag and leave at room temperature for 48 hours. After two days, remove the bag and allow to dry fully: another 24 hours for a piece this size. The vase is
bone-dry
when it has lightened uniformly and feels cool against the back of the hand rather than cold (the cold spot means moisture is still escaping).
Finishing

The exposed coil ridges are a design feature: do not sand them away. Apply two coats of matt acrylic sealant, working the brush into the ridges so no unsealed clay remains in the grooves between coils. The interior can be left unsealed since this vase holds a smaller container rather than water directly. If you want to use it for fresh flowers without an inner container, line the interior with a thin layer of waterproof tile grout and allow to cure for 48 hours before use.
Variations
Build with two different-coloured clays: roll half the coils from white clay and half from terracotta-coloured clay, alternating them. The colour contrast makes the coil structure more pronounced.
For a square-section vessel, place coils in a square rather than circular plan, pressing the corners flat with the wooden rib on each layer.

Coil building stacks rings of clay. Each ring joins to the one below. It is one of the oldest ways to make large pots. Most teaching says smooth the outside so the coils hide. This tutorial does the opposite. The coils stay visible on the outside as a spiral ridge. Only the inside wall is smoothed. This keeps the form strong. The finished piece shows how it was built.

rows.problem: Coils separate from each other during drying
rows.cause: Slurry not applied to both surfaces before joining; interior join not blended
rows.fix: Score and apply slurry to both contact surfaces. Blend the interior join immediately after placing each coil: this is the structural bond.

rows.problem: Form collapses inward as it builds upward
rows.cause: Lower coils not stiffened enough before adding weight above
rows.fix: Wait for the lower half to reach leather-hard before continuing. Cover the top with a damp cloth during the wait to prevent the join edge drying out.

rows.problem: Exterior ridges crack horizontally between coils
rows.cause: Coils at different moisture levels when joined; upper coil drier than lower
rows.fix: Keep all clay in a sealed bag between sessions. Roll each coil fresh from the same bag immediately before use.
